summary: A Best Current Practice document that defines how media feature tags are registered, using IANA as the central registry for the media feature vocabulary. It lets different systems describe their capabilities with a shared set of names.

eli5.summary: Devices need a common dictionary to say what they can do, like show color or print big pages. This document says how new words get added to that dictionary.

questions: how to register a media feature tag

what is the global tree for media feature tags
subtitle: How a shared vocabulary of device and content capabilities gets names, owners and a registry.

tldr.problem: Applications such as the Web connect very different clients, servers and data formats, and they need a common vocabulary to say what a party can display, print or handle.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines media feature tags, a syntax and a list of value types for them, three kinds of registration tree with different review rules, and a registration template filed with IANA as the central registry.
tldr.outcome: Anyone can propose a tag, and tags in the URI tree need no registration at all. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 31) and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 2506 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 31) from March 1999, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself points to related work such as RFC 2534, which defines example media feature tags for display, print and fax.

sections.title: Why a Shared Vocabulary
sections.content:
Recent Internet applications, such as the World Wide Web, tie together a great diversity in data formats, client and server platforms and communities. That creates a need for ways to describe and negotiate media features, so that information can be matched to the capabilities and preferences of the parties involved.

Extensible negotiation mechanisms need a common vocabulary to identify features without ambiguity. RFC 2506 defines a registration process and an authority for that vocabulary, with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as the central registry. It also defines a URI tree so that feature definitions can be shared without any registration.
sections.eli5: If two computers want to agree on how to show a page, they need to use the same words for things like screen colors. This document makes sure there is one official word list.

sections.title: What a Media Feature Tag Is
sections.content:
A media feature tag names one individual, simple characteristic related to media capabilities or to properties of the resource it is applied to. Examples in the RFC are the color depth of a screen, the type of paper available in a printer, the fonts available to a recipient and the ability to display graphical content.

Each tag identifies a single characteristic, and any value it carries must use the data type defined for that tag. Bigger needs, such as the width and height of a display, are met by composing several tags into a feature collection, which is described elsewhere.

The registry has limits. It presumes the MIME media type registry exists, and MIME media types MUST NOT be re-registered as media feature tags. It is limited to tags that express a capability or preference about how content is presented. A tag already used by one protocol MAY be registered if it might be applied outside its current domain.
sections.eli5: A tag is one small fact about a device, like 'can show pictures'. For bigger facts, like screen width and height, you use two tags together.

sections.title: Tag Syntax
sections.content:
A tag is a string of US-ASCII uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits and the characters colon, slash, dot, percent and dash. Tags are case-insensitive and should begin with a letter. The RFC gives the grammar in ABNF.

Dots may imply hierarchy: a feature can be subtyped as tree.feature.subfeature, and the registration says so. Because a letter followed by a dot marks a registration tree, registrants should avoid inventing tags that begin that way, so they do not collide with trees created later.
sections.eli5: Tags are written with a small set of ordinary keyboard characters. A dot works like a folder separator, so names that start with one letter and a dot are reserved for groups.

sections.title: Tag Values and Units
sections.content:
The registry initially supports six kinds of value: signed integers, rational numbers, tokens with an equality relationship, tokens with a defined ordering, strings compared octet by octet, and strings with a defined equality or comparison. At registration each tag is tied to a single data type. If that type implies a comparison or an ordering, the registrant must define it, either by listing the tokens in order or by pointing to an ordering mechanism.

Tags about spatial or temporal characteristics must be registered with a single canonical unit. SI units are strongly preferred. Where practice uses another system, such as pixels per inch, the registrant must give a conversion method to SI, and it should include a rounding practice.

Some protocols identify capabilities with ASN.1 identifiers instead of readable names. A registrant may supply one or ask IANA to assign one, but it is not required for registration.
sections.eli5: Each tag holds one kind of answer, such as a number, a word or yes/no. If the answer is a measurement, the rules say which unit to use so everyone counts the same way.

sections.title: Registration Trees
sections.content:
Tags are registered in trees, told apart by faceted names of the form tree.feature-name. Each tree has its own review requirements, using the vocabulary of the IANA considerations guidelines.

  • IETF tree: for tags of general interest. It needs IETF Consensus, IESG approval and publication of the tag specification as an RFC. Names normally contain no dot.
  • Global tree: names start with g.. It needs Expert Review by a designated expert, and anyone with a need to communicate about a capability or preference may propose a tag. An organization may use a name such as g.organization.blinktags, and should reuse the name it holds in the MIME vendor tree.
  • URI tree: names start with u. followed by a URI. The author of the URI is the registration authority for the feature, and these tags are considered unregistered. No review is required.

IANA may also create new top-level trees, with the advice and consent of the IESG, for example for scientific societies. Such trees are announced by an IESG-approved RFC.
sections.eli5: There are three shelves in the dictionary. One is for words everyone agrees on, one is for company words checked by an expert, and one is for words you write down yourself on your own website.

sections.title: How IANA Handles Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registers an IETF tree tag only after the IESG says the registration has been approved. A global tree tag is registered after a designated expert confirms it meets the technical requirements of the RFC. IANA decides whether a proposed global-tree designation is acceptable, and may ask the organization for a new proposal.

Registrations are posted in an anonymous FTP directory and listed in the periodically issued Assigned Numbers RFC (at the time, STD 2, RFC 1700). The description and supporting material may also be published as an Informational RFC.
sections.eli5: The keeper of the dictionary only writes a word in after the right people say yes. Then the new word is posted where everyone can look it up.

sections.title: The Registration Template
sections.content:
A registration is an email to the media feature tags mailing list with the subject Registration of media feature tag XXXX, filled in from a template. It asks for the tag name, an optional ASN.1 identifier (or the value New assignment by IANA), and a summary of no more than 4 lines.

The registrant states whether the tag is Boolean (TRUE means the capability is available, FALSE that it is not) or has a numeric or enumerated value of exactly one of the six data types. Contact details, the change controller and the intended usage are required, and the usage is one of COMMON, LIMITED USE or OBSOLETE. A security section asks about privacy, denial of service from incorrect values, and other concerns. Many other fields are optional.

A publication delay of at most two months may be requested for the global or IETF trees. It delays only official publication, not discussion on the mailing list.
sections.eli5: To add a word you fill in a form: its name, what it means, what kind of answer it takes, and who to ask about it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is short. Negotiation mechanisms reveal information about one party to other parties. That may raise privacy concerns, and it may let a malicious party make better guesses about whether specific security holes are present.
sections.eli5: When a device tells others what it can do, it also gives away clues about itself, so it should think about who is listening.
